courses.title: Git & GitHub Crash Course
courses.summary: Version control is non-negotiable for modern developers. This crash course takes you from zero to confidently using Git on the command line and collaborating on GitHub.

sections.heading: Why Git?
sections.body: Git is a distributed version control system. It tracks every change to your code, lets you experiment in branches, and makes collaboration possible without overwriting each other's work. Every professional codebase uses it.

sections.heading: The Core Commands
sections.body: git init creates a new repo. git clone copies a remote repo. git status shows what changed. git add stages changes. git commit saves a snapshot. git push uploads to the remote. git pull downloads and merges.

sections.heading: Branching & Merging
sections.body: Branches let you work in isolation. git branch feature creates a branch; git checkout feature switches to it. Make commits, then git merge feature back into main. Pull requests on GitHub make this reviewable.

sections.heading: Handling Conflicts
sections.body: Conflicts happen when two branches change the same lines. Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>. Open the file, pick the resolution, save, and commit. Stay calm — conflicts are normal.

courses.code:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "initial commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git push -u origin main

# feature branch flow
git checkout -b feature/login
git commit -am "add login"
git push origin feature/login
# open PR on GitHub, then merge
git checkout main
git pull origin main

courses.title: Tailwind CSS Crash Course
courses.summary: Utility-first CSS that lets you build modern UIs without writing CSS files. Learn the mental model, the most common utilities, and how to extract reusable components.

sections.heading: The Utility-First Mental Model
sections.body: Instead of naming classes like .card and writing CSS, you compose utilities directly in markup: class="bg-white rounded-xl p-4 shadow". It feels verbose at first, but you never context-switch to a CSS file, and your styles are co-located with the markup they affect.

sections.heading: Spacing, Color & Typography
sections.body: p-4 = padding 1rem. m-2 = margin 0.5rem. gap-4 = gap 1rem. Colors use scales: bg-purple-600, text-gray-300. Text sizes: text-sm, text-lg, text-2xl. Font weights: font-normal, font-bold.

sections.heading: Responsive & State Variants
sections.body: Prefix utilities with breakpoints: md:flex-row applies flex-row at medium screens. State prefixes: hover:bg-purple-700, focus:ring-2, disabled:opacity-50. Dark mode: dark:bg-gray-900.

sections.heading: Extracting Components
sections.body: When utilities repeat, extract them. In React/Vue, that's a component. In plain HTML, use @apply in your CSS to compose utilities into a named class. Don't extract too early — duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

courses.code:
Title

Description text.

/* extract with @apply */ .btn-primary { @apply bg-purple-600 hover:bg-purple-700 text-white font-semibold py-2 px-4 rounded-lg transition; }

courses.title: Algorithms Crash Course
courses.summary: The algorithms that show up in every interview and in real-world code: sorting, searching, recursion, and dynamic programming. Visual, intuitive, no math degree required.

sections.heading: Big-O in One Minute
sections.body: Big-O describes how runtime grows with input. O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear, O(n log n) sorting, O(n²) nested loops, O(2^n) naive recursion. Always ask: as n grows, what matters?

sections.heading: Binary Search
sections.body: On a sorted array, binary search halves the search space each step — O(log n). Most bugs come from off-by-one in the boundary. Use lo <= hi and mid = (lo + hi) >> 1.

sections.heading: Recursion & Backtracking
sections.body: Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller version of itself. Always define a base case. Backtracking explores all options and undels choices — classic for permutations, combinations, and puzzles like N-Queens.

sections.heading: Dynamic Programming
sections.body: DP caches subproblem results to avoid recomputation. Two flavors: top-down with memoization, bottom-up with a table. Identify the state, the transition, and the base case. Practice on Fibonacci, knapsack, and longest common subsequence.

courses.title: SQL Crash Course
courses.summary: Speak to databases. SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, subqueries, and window functions — everything you need to query real data and ship features that touch a database.

sections.heading: The SELECT Statement
sections.body: SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT caps the count. SELECT * is fine for exploration but always specify columns in production code.

sections.heading: JOINs
sections.body: JOINs combine rows from two tables on a key. INNER JOIN keeps only matches. LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows. RIGHT and FULL JOINs exist but are less common. Always qualify columns when joining: users.name.

sections.heading: Aggregation & GROUP BY
sections.body: Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY groups rows by a column before aggregating. HAVING filters groups (WHERE filters rows before grouping).

sections.heading: Window Functions
sections.body: Window functions compute across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, and SUM() OVER() are the workhorses for analytics queries.

courses.code:
-- basic select
SELECT name, email, created_at
FROM users
WHERE active = true
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- join with aggregation
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.total) AS spent
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.country = 'KE'
GROUP BY u.name
HAVING SUM(o.total) > 1000
ORDER BY spent DESC;

-- window function
SELECT name, salary,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
  AVG(salary) OVER () AS team_avg
FROM employees;

courses.title: Regex Crash Course
courses.summary: Regular expressions are a mini-language for matching text. Learn the syntax, the metacharacters, and the common patterns every developer should recognize.

sections.heading: The Basics
sections.body: Letters and digits match themselves. . matches any char. * means zero or more, + means one or more, ? means optional. ^ anchors to start, $ anchors to end. Use \d, \w, \s for digit, word char, whitespace.

sections.heading: Character Classes & Groups
sections.body: [abc] matches a, b, or c. [^abc] matches anything except. (ab) groups; (?:ab) non-capturing. | means or: cat|dog matches either. Quantifiers: {3} exactly 3, {2,5} between 2 and 5.

sections.heading: Common Patterns
sections.body: Email: ^[\w.-]+@[\w.-]+\.\w+$. Phone (KE): ^(\+?254|0)\d{9}$. URL, date, password strength — every developer should have these memorized or bookmarked.

sections.heading: When NOT to Use Regex
sections.body: Don't parse HTML or XML with regex — use a parser. If your regex is longer than a tweet, it's probably wrong. Test with regex101.com and add tests for edge cases.
